item.title: Dazaifu Tenmangu: Shrine of Learning — Guide
item.description: Dazaifu Tenmangu, just outside Fukuoka city, is one of the most revered shrines in Japan, dedicated to Sugawara no Michizane, the Heian-era scholar-official deified as Tenjin, the god of learning. Students from across the country come to pray for success in exams, and the beautiful grounds are famous for their plum trees — Michizane’s favourite — which bloom in late winter, including a legendary ‘flying plum’ said to have flown from Kyoto to be near him.

item.title: Kishu Ume: Japan's Finest Plums and Umeboshi — Guide
item.description: Wakayama produces the majority of Japan’s ume (Japanese plum), and its Nanko-ume variety, grown above all around Minabe, is considered the finest in the country — large, thin-skinned and fleshy, making umeboshi of exceptional quality. The plum orchards blanket the hills behind the coast, and in February the Minabe-Bairin grove erupts into what locals call ‘a million plum blossoms’, filling the valley with white flowers and scent. Beyond the blossoms, the region offers umeboshi tastings of every degree of saltiness and sweetness, plum wine, and factory visits explaining the long pickling process.

item.title: Wakayama Events & Festivals: Fire Festivals, Plum Blossom Season & Traditional Celebrations
item.description: Wakayama’s festival calendar is shaped by two things that define the prefecture itself: ancient religious tradition and agricultural cycle. The Kumano Grand Shrines have been hosting ritual ceremonies without interruption for over 1,500 years; the mountain valleys have been marking planting, harvest, and the seasons with community events for as long as anyone can trace. The result is a calendar of genuinely un-performed events — festivals that exist because communities have always done them, not because a tourism board decided a festival would attract visitors.
